title: SUDEP: sudden unexpected death in epilepsy
intro: SUDEP is the sudden, unexpected death of a person with epilepsy who was otherwise well, not caused by an accident, drowning or a known cause. It is rare but is the leading cause of epilepsy-related death. Although fearful, understanding the risks lets people with epilepsy and their families take steps that may lower the chance.

sections.heading: What is known
paragraphs: SUDEP often occurs at night or during sleep and frequently follows a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but it may involve disturbed breathing, heart rhythm and brain function after a seizure. It is estimated to affect a small number of people with epilepsy each year, with much higher risk when seizures are frequent and uncontrolled.

sections.heading: Risk factors
paragraphs: The strongest risk factor is frequent tonic-clonic seizures, especially at night. Others include having epilepsy for many years, not taking medicine regularly, drinking excessive alcohol, sleeping alone without supervision and taking multiple anti-seizure medicines because seizures are hard to control. Young adults appear to be at the highest risk.

sections.heading: Reducing the risk
paragraphs: Controlling seizures is the most important step. Take medicines exactly as prescribed, avoid sleep deprivation and heavy alcohol, and keep regular appointments to review treatment. If seizures continue despite medication, ask about other treatment such as surgery, nerve stimulation or alternative medicines. Night-time supervision, bed alarms or monitoring devices may help some people.

sections.heading: First aid for seizures
paragraphs: Family members can learn seizure first aid. After a convulsion, turn the person onto their side, make sure the airway is clear, stay with them and call emergency help if the seizure lasts more than five minutes or breathing does not resume. Learning resuscitation can be life-saving.

sections.heading: Talking about it
paragraphs: Many doctors feel hesitant to discuss SUDEP, but experts recommend that all people with epilepsy and their families be informed about it in a supportive, balanced way. Ask your neurologist about your personal risk. Support groups and epilepsy organisations offer information and bereavement support.

examples.title: Reviewing treatment
examples.text: Imagine you still have night-time seizures despite medicine. You could ask your neurologist whether treatment can be adjusted or other options explored.

examples.title: Learning first aid
examples.text: Suppose you live with someone who has epilepsy. You might attend a first-aid course that includes seizure management and resuscitation.

questions: What is my personal risk of SUDEP, and how can it be lowered?
Are there other treatments that could control my seizures better?
Should we use night-time monitoring, and what first aid should my family know?
